bioinfo.title: Mechanistic gene-regulation-based trajectory inference with bowside
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract While single-cell RNA sequencing enables the in-depth study of differentiation processes, simultaneous trajectory inference and gene regulatory network reconstruction remain challenging. We propose bowside, a shallow neural stochastic differentiation model that mechanistically models gene regulation. Our method successfully recovers gene expression trends and the underlying regulatory interactions. We demonstrate bowside on hematopoiesis and induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming data, retrieving known fate-determining network motifs.

bioinfo.title: Optimal transport reveals unresolved cells in single-cell multi-omics
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell multi-omics methods align cells across modalities, integrate them into one embedding and transfer labels between them. All three steps depend on a match between cells in two modalities, but this match usually stays hidden inside each tool. Its errors are hidden too, and every cell looks equally certain. Here we make the match explicit. For each pair of datasets, we build a soft coupling matrix with optimal transport and use it in three ways beyond estimating the match itself: to score how uncertain each cell’s match is, to upgrade existing integration and label-transfer tools without retraining them, and to decide which cells to set aside. Across 78 dataset pairs spanning six modality combinations, we evaluated ten integration and ten label-transfer tools using matched random removal as the control. We developed an ensemble coupling achieving the most accurate recovery of true cell pairs. Feeding couplings back into the tools improved label transfer clearly but improved integration only in how well the modalities mix. The ambiguity score, which we computed as a group-vote margin, gave the larger and more consistent gain in both tasks. Ambiguous-flagged cells matched worse in almost every dataset and removing them beat random removal in 98% of integration tests and 91% of label-transfer comparisons. These hard-to-integrate cells are mostly among rare, transitional and poorly measured populations. Making correspondence explicit therefore provides a practical way to distinguish reliable cross-modality results from uncertain ones while flagging cells that might have important roles in development and disease.

bioinfo.title: Multi-omics-constrained kinetic models quantify pathway rewiring and predict metabolic vulnerabilities in BRCA1-deficient ovarian cancer.
bioinfo.abstract: Time-resolved, network-wide consequences of cancer metabolic reprogramming remain poorly understood. We built multi-omics-constrained, near-genome-scale kinetic ensembles for isogenic BRCA1 wild-type and BRCA1-mutant ovarian cancer cells. Covering over 2,100 reactions, the ensembles enabled uncertainty-quantified simulations of nutrient, metabolite, and enzyme perturbations. Metabolic control analysis identified 28 enzyme-mediated vulnerabilities; 24 are linked to experimental or approved DrugBank compounds, whereas four lack documented drug associations. Independent DepMap data supported a subset of these candidates. All 28 emerged directly from the mechanistic model structure and multi-omics constraints, with no calibration to known drug targets or cancer-dependency data. Simulations of thymidylate synthase, hexokinase, and triokinase inhibition predicted target- and physiology-specific changes in pathway use, energy metabolism, and a shared ceramide-linked stress response. Mapping predicted enzyme-activity shifts to BRCA1-associated transcription factors suggested regulatory routes underlying differences between the two states. These ensembles provide a reusable framework for time-resolved, mechanistic hypothesis generation across cancers and other diseases. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

bioinfo.title: A Multi-modal LLM-Knowledge Fusion Framework for Predicting Single-cell Genetic Perturbation Effects
bioinfo.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding cellular responses to genetic perturbations is fundamental for drug discovery, yet experimental approaches face significant limitations in coverage and cost that prevent comprehensive mapping of cellular behavior. This has motivated the development of virtual cells—computational models that learn the relationship between cell state and function to predict the consequences of perturbations across diverse contexts. However, current computational methods suffer from limited accuracy in complex genetic interactions, poor biological interpretability, and inadequate generalization to unseen genes, severely constraining virtual cell capabilities. We present scPert, a multi-modal framework based on Transformer architecture that integrates large language model embeddings with structured biological knowledge to predict single-cell transcriptomic responses to genetic perturbations. Through hierarchical fusion of knowledge graph representations, contextual embeddings from foundation models, and gene-specific encodings, scPert achieves significant performance improvements in both single-gene and combinatorial perturbations over existing methods. In cancer-relevant applications, scPert demonstrates the capability to reveal p53 pathway dynamics and immune checkpoint regulatory mechanisms. Systematic evaluation on 42 cancer dependency genes demonstrates scPert’s ability to identify critical potential therapeutic targets. Our framework establishes a powerful computational foundation for virtual cell construction and accelerates drug target discovery.

bioinfo.title: An interpretable Graph-Regularized Optimal Transport Framework for Diagonal Single-Cell Integrative Analysis
bioinfo.abstract: BACKGROUND: Recent advancements in single-cell omics technologies have enabled detailed characterization of cellular processes. However, coassay sequencing technologies remain limited, resulting in unpaired single-cell omics datasets with differing feature dimensions. FINDING: We present GROTIA (Graph-Regularized Optimal Transport Framework for Diagonal Single-Cell Integrative Analysis), a computational method to align multi-omics datasets without requiring any prior correspondence information. GROTIA achieves global alignment through optimal transport while preserving local relationships via graph regularization. Additionally, our approach provides interpretability by deriving domain-specific feature importance from partial derivatives, highlighting key biological markers. Moreover, the transport plan between modalities can be leveraged for post-integration clustering, enabling a data-driven approach to discover novel cell subpopulations. CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrate GROTIA's superior performance on four simulated and four real-world datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art unsupervised alignment methods and confirming the biological significance of the top features identified in each domain.

bioinfo.title: Chronic metabolic stress drives developmental programs and loss of tissue functions in non-transformed liver that mirror tumor states and stratify survival
bioinfo.abstract: Under chronic stress, cells must balance competing demands between cellular survival and tissue function. In metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly NAFLD/NASH), hepatocytes cooperate with structural and immune cells to perform crucial metabolic, synthetic, and detoxification functions despite nutrient imbalances. While prior work has emphasized stress-induced drivers of cell death, the dynamic adaptations of surviving cells and their functional repercussions remain unclear. Namely, we do not know which pathways and programs define cellular responses, what regulatory factors mediate (mal)adaptations, and how this aberrant activity connects to tissue-scale dysfunction and long-term disease outcomes. Here, by applying longitudinal single-cell multi-omics to a mouse model of chronic metabolic stress and extending to human cohorts, we show that stress drives survival-linked tradeoffs and metabolic rewiring, manifesting as shifts towards development-associated states in non-transformed hepatocytes with accompanying decreases in their professional functionality. Diet-induced adaptations occur significantly prior to tumorigenesis but parallel tumorigenesis-induced phenotypes and predict worsened human cancer survival. Through the development of a multi-omic computational gene regulatory inference framework and human in vitro and mouse in vivo genetic perturbations, we validate transcriptional (RELB, SOX4) and metabolic (HMGCS2) mediators that co-regulate and couple the balance between developmental state and hepatocyte functional identity programming. Our work defines cellular features of liver adaptation to chronic stress as well as their links to long-term disease outcomes and cancer hallmarks, unifying diverse axes of cellular dysfunction around core causal mechanisms.

bioinfo.title: Genetic Perturbation Prediction Models Fail Out-of-Distribution: A Rigorous Benchmark and Systematic Evaluation
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Perturbation prediction models - which forecast transcriptional responses to gene inactivation - are increasingly proposed as in silico surrogates for genome-scale drug discovery screens. Yet, rigorous evaluation of whether these models genuinely generalize beyond their training distribution has been lacking. Existing benchmarks rely predominantly on random train-test splits, obscuring systematic failure modes that only emerge under realistic out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. Here we introduce EL-PERTURB (Extrapolative Learning for PERTURBation Prediction), a benchmarking framework that stress-tests 20 perturbation prediction models spanning six architecture classes on both essential gene and genome-wide Perturb- seq screens, using a novel stratified OOD splitting strategy that partitions train and test sets into functionally distinct regions of transcriptional space. We find that model performance degrades substantially under OOD conditions, and that architectural complexity - including single-cell foundation model embeddings - confers no reliable advantage over well-tuned simpler baselines. EL-PERTURB establishes a rigorous benchmark for perturbation effect prediction across a gradient of generalization difficulty, providing a guide for building models that can genuinely serve as surrogates for wet-lab screening.

bioinfo.title: scCody distinguishes aging-aligned from divergent disease-associated cellular remodeling
bioinfo.abstract: Biological aging clocks summarize molecular changes as a single age estimate, but cannot distinguish disease-associated changes that follow healthy aging from those that deviate from it. Here we introduce scCody, a generative framework that learns age-dependent cellular population dynamics from cross-sectional single-cell cohorts using population-level optimal transport and endpoint-consistency regularization. scCody accurately reconstructed cellular populations at unseen ages, recovered age-associated transcriptional changes more effectively than existing generative dynamics models, and enabled donor-age inference without direct age-regression training. Using the learned healthy aging reference, scCody decomposed disease-associated cellular displacement into aging-aligned and orthogonal components. In Alzheimer's disease, selected neuronal populations showed substantial aging-aligned remodeling alongside shared orthogonal changes associated with established pathology signatures. In contrast, COVID-19 exhibited weaker aging alignment and more pronounced orthogonal immune remodeling. Further decomposition revealed patient-level interferon variation associated with symptom duration and increased transcriptional heterogeneity in CD16 monocytes. This framework provides an extension of biological age assessment beyond a single age estimate, distinguishing cellular changes that resemble healthy aging from those that depart from it.

bioinfo.title: scPhyloGRN: gene regulatory network inference guided by lineage topology in single-cell developmental data.
bioinfo.abstract: Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference from single-cell transcriptomes is complicated by expression patterns associated with both cell state and shared ancestry. Cellular phylogenies provide developmental context, but incorporating relationships among individual cells into gene-level regulatory inference remains challenging. We present scPhyloGRN, a supervised framework that integrates single-cell gene expression with cellular phylogeny to prioritize directed transcription factor (TF)-target candidates within the observed gene set. The framework maps cell ancestry to gene associations that guide graph construction, attention in a dual-stream encoder, and lineage-consistency regularization. We evaluated scPhyloGRN against ten methods across 17 dataset-reference settings spanning four mouse embryos and one Caenorhabditis elegans dataset. scPhyloGRN showed an overall advantage in regulatory edge prioritization, supported by additional evaluations using shared candidate spaces. Removing lineage information reduced AUPRC in the ablation analyses, while branch-level and regulator-level analyses showed improved ranking and recovery of reference-supported regulatory candidates. Source code and analysis workflows are available at https://github.com/Maria0852/scPhyloGRN, with a versioned archive at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22793831.

bioinfo.title: BioTrajX: evaluating biological plausibility in single-cell trajectory inference
bioinfo.abstract: ABSTRACT Summary Trajectory inference (TI) methods reconstruct cellular progression from single-cell RNA sequencing data, typically by ordering cells along a pseudotime axis. However, different TI methods and analytical choices can produce divergent trajectories from the same dataset, making it difficult to determine which inferred trajectory best reflects the underlying biological process. Existing evaluation strategies often rely on computational benchmarks or qualitative biological assessment, with limited standardized approaches for incorporating a priori biological knowledge. Here, we present BioTrajX, an R package for biologically informed evaluation of pseudotime trajectories using three complementary metrics: Directionality (D), which measures agreement between pseudotime and expected biological progression; Order Consistency (O), which quantifies the coherence of marker-program changes along the trajectory; and Endpoint Validity (E), which assesses enrichment of expected cell states at trajectory endpoints. Together, the DOE metrics provide an interpretable framework for comparing alternative trajectory inference results and evaluating root-cell choices prior to downstream analyses. Availability and Implementation BioTrajX is implemented in R and freely available under the MIT License at https://github.com/irislity/BioTrajX . Code for reproducing the analyses and figures is available at https://github.com/irislity/BioTrajX_manuscript . Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

bioinfo.title: Deep Lineage: Single-cell lineage tracing and fate inference using deep learning.
bioinfo.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing and lineage tracing techniques have provided valuable insights into the temporal changes in gene expression during development, tumor progression, and disease onset. However, there are few computational methods available to analyze this information to help understand multicellular dynamics. We introduce Deep Lineage, a deep-learning method for analyzing time-series single-cell RNA sequencing with matched lineage tracing data. Our method accurately predicts early cell fate biases and gene expression profiles at different time points within a clone, surpassing existing methods in fate prediction accuracy. We further validate our model using LineageSim, a fate-aware lineage simulator, demonstrating robustness to technical noise such as barcode dropout and clone misidentification. Additionally, we apply Deep Lineage to in silico perturbations in cellular reprogramming and hematopoiesis to identify key genes and pathways associated with cell fate determination and propose testable perturbation hypotheses for experimental follow-up.

bioinfo.title: scMultiPreDICT: A single-cell predictive framework with transcriptomic and epigenetic signatures
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Cellular responses to genetic perturbations depend on both transcriptional programs and the epigenetic landscape. While single-cell multiomics technologies enable simultaneous profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility, the relative contribution of each regulatory layer to gene expression remains unclear. Existing computational approaches focus on data integration and gene regulatory network inference but do not systematically compare the predictive performance of transcriptional versus epigenetic features on a gene-by-gene basis. We present scMultiPreDICT, a computational framework for comparative predictive modeling of gene expression using single-cell multiomics data. scMultiPreDICT benchmarks RNA-only, ATAC-only and multimodal feature sets across six machine learning models including regression, tree-based learning and deep learning using multiple biological datasets. We show that RNA-derived features generally provide strong predictive power, whereas chromatin accessibility alone yields a modest performance. Surprisingly, multimodal integration does not uniformly improve prediction accuracy; instead, its benefit is gene-specific and context-dependent. Feature importance analysis reveals that transcriptional features dominate for most genes, whereas chromatin accessibility contributes meaningfully for a subset of genes in specific cellular contexts. Overall, the results demonstrate that regulatory layers contribute differently to gene expression. scMultiPreDICT provides a systematic framework for identifying the relative contributions of transcriptional and epigenetic regulation across genes and cellular contexts, guiding the design of targeted perturbation studies and the prioritization of regulatory layers for therapeutic interventions. scMultiPreDICT is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/UzunLab/scMultiPreDICT/ .

bioinfo.title: OT-knn: a neighborhood-aware optimal transport framework for aligning spatial transcriptomics data
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression while preserving spatial context within tissues, enabling detailed characterization of tissue organization. As ST technologies advance, aligning datasets across tissue sections, individuals, platforms, and developmental stages has become increasingly important but remains challenging due to sparse expression, biological heterogeneity, and geometric distortions between slices. We introduce OT-knn, a method for ST alignment that integrates local neighborhood information within an optimal transport framework. Rather than relying solely on single-spot expression, OT-knn reconstructs each spot using its spatial k -nearest neighbors, capturing microenvironment context that is more robust to noise and variability. These representations are then used to derive probabilistic correspondences between slices. We evaluate OT-knn using simulated data with known ground-truth alignment and real datasets from multiple ST platforms, including human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex data (10x Genomics Visium), mouse brain aging data with both within-donor and cross-donor comparisons (MERFISH), a multi-stage axolotl brain dataset (Stereo-seq), and a cross-platform analysis using mouse embryo datasets profiled by Stereo-seq and seqFISH. Across these settings, OT-knn achieves accurate and robust alignment, particularly in the presence of spatial deformation, donor heterogeneity, developmental variation and technological differences. Author summary Understanding how cells are arranged within tissues is important for studying how organs develop, age, and respond to disease. Spatial transcriptomics is a new technology that measures gene activity while keeping track of where each measurement comes from in the tissue. However, comparing data from different tissue slices, different individuals, or different time points is difficult. Tissues can change shape during preparation, gene measurements can be noisy, and natural biological differences exist across samples. In this work, we develop a method to better match corresponding regions across tissue slices. Instead of looking at each location by itself, we also consider information from its surrounding neighborhood. This provides a more stable and informative view of the tissue and makes it easier to match similar regions, even when the data are imperfect or the tissue shapes differ. We test our method on both simulated and real datasets from human, mouse, and axolotl brain tissues. Our approach enables more reliable comparisons of spatial gene activity across samples, which can help researchers study development, aging, and disease.

bioinfo.title: Causal chambers as a real-world physical testbed for AI methodology
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract In some fields of artificial intelligence, machine learning and statistics, the validation of new methods and algorithms is often hindered by the scarcity of suitable real-world datasets. Researchers must often turn to simulated data, which yields limited information about the applicability of the proposed methods to real problems. As a step forward, we have constructed two devices that allow us to quickly and inexpensively produce large datasets from non-trivial but well-understood physical systems. The devices, which we call causal chambers, are computer-controlled laboratories that allow us to manipulate and measure an array of variables from these physical systems, providing a rich testbed for algorithms from a variety of fields. We illustrate potential applications through a series of case studies in fields such as causal discovery, out-of-distribution generalization, change point detection, independent component analysis and symbolic regression. For applications to causal inference, the chambers allow us to carefully perform interventions. We also provide and empirically validate a causal model of each chamber, which can be used as ground truth for different tasks. The hardware and software are made open source, and the datasets are publicly available at causalchamber.org or through the Python package causalchamber .

bioinfo.title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distin-guish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.

bioinfo.title: Identifiable inverse optimal transport for single-cell state transitions
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Signed effects of target-state programmes are unidentifiable in balanced optimal transport because fixed endpoint distributions make their contributions constant across feasible plans. We introduce UOT-IOT, a semi-relaxed inverse transport framework that restores measurable target-mass responses and provides a rank condition for local identifiability. It recovers coefficients in ground-truth benchmarks (correlation 0.997 versus 0.081 for balanced transport), transfers frozen directions to six unseen samples with specificity controls, and achieves the lowest transition error against seven methods under matched evaluation conditions. GH-IOT separates shared directions from context and lineage-history offsets, revealing opposing history-associated effects. IFN/HLA is associated with patient treatment response, whereas EMT relates to drug sensitivity and perturbation-induced state changes. PERSIST-IOT improves future population-composition prediction in an independent experiment. Together, these modules distinguish current state, transition propensity and future population outcomes while supporting testable biological interpretations.

bioinfo.title: Graph-guided flow matching enables biologically informed prediction at single-cell resolution
bioinfo.abstract: Perturb-seq enables systematic interrogation of massively parallel genetic perturbations at single-cell resolution, yet exhaustive characterization of the full perturbation space remains impractical. Here, we present Graph-guided Flow Matching (GFM), a generative framework that integrates biological knowledge graphs with latent flow matching to predict post-perturbation single-cell transcriptomes. Across multiple large-scale Perturb-seq datasets, GFM outperforms a strong linear baseline and current deep-learning models in predicting unseen single-gene perturbations, while training up to 30x faster and remaining robust with limited training data. GFM also demonstrates competitive performance in the two-gene perturbation prediction task when neither perturbed gene is observed during training. Ablation experiments show that combining flow matching with knowledge graphs enables accurate prediction of perturbation responses. Finally, GFM accurately calculates transcriptional consequences of HSP90AA1 inactivation and identifies target candidates unseen by the model in chronic myeloid leukemia. Our study establishes GFM as a biologically informed generative framework that predicts single-cell perturbation responses for prioritization of therapeutic targets.

bioinfo.title: DECODER-SC: A single-cell algorithm for quantifying transcription factor-target regulatory discordance.
bioinfo.abstract: Existing transcription factor (TF) activity inference methods quantify regulatory potential but do not evaluate whether inferred TF activity is concordant with downstream target-gene expression. To address this limitation, we present DECODER-SC, a single-cell algorithm that quantifies TF-target regulatory discordance from single-cell RNA-sequencing data. DECODER-SC integrates direction-aware regulatory logic using DoRothEA activation and repression annotations, weighted discordance scoring, and permutation-based statistical inference to compute TF-level, interaction-level, and cell-level discordance metrics. Benchmarking against AUCell, VIPER, and TF-target correlation baseline demonstrated that discordance profiles capture regulatory structure not explained by activity magnitude or simple expression co-variation. Ablation analysis supported the contribution of activator/repressor-aware modeling to discordance detection, while robustness analyses demonstrated highly stable TF rankings across multiple threshold settings. Orthogonal Perturb-seq validation demonstrated a reproducible IRF1 discordance signal across experimental units (effect = 0.0643, 95% CI = 0.0441-0.0845, BH-adjusted P = 0.0235). Leave-one-target-out and VIPER-based sensitivity analyses confirmed that discordance classifications are robust to target-level circularity and alternative TF-activity inference (97.76% and 73.42% agreement, respectively). Replicate-aware sample-level analysis further showed that cell-level proliferation and pathway associations were exploratory rather than statistically independent. Application of DECODER-SC across multiple single-cell transcriptomic datasets identified recurrent regulatory discordance patterns associated with malignant progression, stress-adaptive transcriptional programs, and transitional cellular states. DECODER-SC expands current single-cell regulatory analysis by enabling systematic quantification of TF-target discordance across heterogeneous cellular populations.

bioinfo.title: Single-cell transcriptomics in nutrition and metabolic research: Current approaches and emerging applications
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics has emerged as a transformative approach for investigating cellular heterogeneity, nutrient-responsive signaling, and metabolic adaptation at unprecedented resolution. Unlike conventional bulk transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables characterization of cell-type-specific gene expression, dynamic cellular states, intercellular communication, and regulatory networks underlying nutrient metabolism in health and disease. Recent advances in scRNA-seq and complementary multi-omics technologies have expanded our understanding of how dietary factors and metabolic stress reshape cellular composition and function across key metabolic tissues, including the intestine, liver, adipose tissue, pancreas, skeletal muscle, and immune system. In this review, we summarize major methodological and computational approaches in single-cell transcriptomics, including sequencing platforms, trajectory inference, cell–cell communication analysis, gene regulatory network reconstruction, and integration with epigenomic, spatial transcriptomic, and metabolomic data. We then highlight emerging applications in nutrition and metabolic research, focusing on cellular heterogeneity in glucose and lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, nutrient sensing, inflammatory remodeling, and diet-responsive signaling. Particular attention is given to recent human studies revealing cell-type-specific responses to dietary interventions, caloric restriction, weight loss, and metabolic therapies. We also discuss key technical and analytical challenges, including sequencing depth, dropout events, batch effects, tissue dissociation artifacts, limited temporal resolution, and difficulties linking transcriptional states to dynamic metabolic flux. Although human applications remain relatively limited and are often constrained by small sample sizes and heterogeneous study designs, integration of scRNA-seq with spatial transcriptomics, single-cell multi-omics, metabolic profiling, and artificial intelligence-assisted analyses offers substantial opportunities to bridge molecular mechanisms with individual variation in nutritional responses. Collectively, these advances establish single-cell transcriptomics as a powerful framework for elucidating nutrient–cell interactions and advancing mechanistically informed precision nutrition.

bioinfo.title: Artificial Intelligence and Multi-Omics Integration for Predicting Stem Cell Fate A Conceptual Framework
bioinfo.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and high-throughput sequencing technologies have transformed stem cell research by enabling comprehensive characterization of cellular states at single-cell resolution. Despite these developments, integrating heterogeneous multi-omics datasets into predictive models of cell fate remains a major challenge. This article proposes a conceptual framework in which artificial intelligence serves as an integrative computational layer linking genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microenvironmental information. Within this framework, stem cell identity is represented as a dynamic multidimensional state, and AI models are used to infer trajectories, identify regulatory interactions, and generate experimentally testable hypotheses. The framework is intended to stimulate interdisciplinary research and does not claim validated predictive performance. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Stem Cells; Multi-Omics; Machine Learning; Systems Biology; Cell Fate Prediction; Computational Biology
bioinfo.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

bioinfo.title: Integrated metabolomic and single-cell analyses reveal crotonylation-related epithelial remodeling and SDC4 dysregulation in adenomyosis.
bioinfo.abstract: Adenomyosis (AM) is characterized by ectopic endometrial invasion and myometrial fibrosis, yet the molecular links between local metabolic remodeling, lysine crotonylation (Kcr), and epithelial dysfunction remain poorly understood. We investigated the metabolic and crotonylation-related landscape of AM and sought to identify epithelial molecular features associated with these alterations. Clinical metabolic profiles, public and newly generated tissue metabolomic data, crotonyl-CoA measurements, and tissue crotonylation assays were integrated with single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses. Kcr-related transcriptional patterns were characterized using multiple gene-set scoring approaches and co-expression analysis, followed by multi-algorithm feature prioritization. SDC4-associated epithelial states were further examined using trajectory inference, cell-cell communication analysis, transcription-factor prediction, and in silico perturbation. Adjusted clinical analyses showed no robust differences in circulating lipid profiles, whereas tissue-level metabolomic analyses revealed alterations in lipid- and lysine-related metabolites in AM. Crotonyl-CoA estimates were higher in AM tissue, accompanied by increased H3K18cr. A higher p65-associated Kcr signal was also observed in a single IP comparison; given that only one IP measurement was available per group, this finding should be considered a preliminary descriptive observation. Single-cell analyses identified prominent Kcr-related transcriptional patterns in epithelial cells and linked this state to adhesion, junctional organization, and epithelial remodeling. SDC4 was consistently prioritized across five machine-learning procedures and was predominantly expressed in epithelial populations. SDC4-positive epithelial cells exhibited distinct inferred differentiation states and intercellular communication patterns, while computational perturbation further implicated SDC4-associated networks in epithelial adhesion, cytoskeletal organization, and junctional regulation. These findings connect local metabolic remodeling and crotonylation-related alterations with a distinct epithelial transcriptional state in AM and identify SDC4 as a consistently prioritized candidate associated with epithelial remodeling. The preliminary p65-associated Kcr observation provides additional context for investigating potential associations among Kcr, p65, and SDC4-related epithelial programs.

bioinfo.title: Fundamental errors in RNA velocity arising from the omission of cell growth
bioinfo.abstract: The ultimate promise of single cell "RNA velocity" methods is compelling: in principle, one can project forward the transcriptional state of each cell and map long-term expression trajectories. While there has been robust and ongoing articulation of limitations of existing methods, consensus frameworks fail to account for a fundamental aspect of cellular dynamics: growth. In a growing population, biomass (including RNA and other macromolecules) is constantly accumulating. This implies a homeostatic velocity (defined in the terms of production and degradation) that is positive, which is at odds with the conventional estimation, interpretation, and uses of velocity. Here, we investigate the consequences of omitting cell growth from the RNA velocity framework. We demonstrate systematic errors that arise in simulations of growing cells and show evidence for these artifacts in existing data. Finally, we point the way forward and highlight that explicitly accounting for cell growth can lead to new biological insights.

bioinfo.title: Predicting cell fate via intelligent porous microcapsules: A multiphysics computational design framework
bioinfo.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Controlled and localized release of biochemical signals is essential for regulating cell differentiation, proliferation, apoptosis, and migration during tissue regeneration. Uncontrolled release can cause adverse effects such as inflammation or fibrotic tissue formation, whereas gradual and spatially confined delivery enables precise modulation of cell behavior. Microcapsule-based systems represent a promising strategy to engineer these interactions. In this study, a multiphysics computational design framework is developed to model the coupled mechanisms of molecular diffusion and fundamental cellular processes within extracellular matrices containing porous microcapsules. METHODS: Molecular release is described using Fick's law, with the membrane modeled as a porous barrier with an effective diffusivity dependent on porosity and thickness. Cell motility is governed by a force-balance formulation, while proliferation and differentiation are regulated by cell deformation and a maturation threshold time dependent on integrated mechanical and chemical stimuli. The model was implemented in a standardized COMSOL and Abaqus environment and validated against Lattice Boltzmann reference data. RESULTS: The model showed excellent agreement with reference data for numerical verification of the transport solver. Parametric analyses indicate that increasing membrane porosity accelerates transport, while thickness acts as a resistive barrier. An empirical design equation was derived to act as a computational surrogate, enabling the a priori selection of structural parameters to match specific tissue maturation windows without experimental trial-and-error. Simulations demonstrate that centrally positioned microcapsules generate synergistic chemical-mechanical cues that maximize the cellular response (15 cells) compared to peripheral configurations. CONCLUSION: The proposed framework provides a predictive computational design tool for the rational design of microstructured delivery systems to optimize tissue regeneration.
bioinfo.venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine

bioinfo.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1–8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9–13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

bioinfo.title: PROFET predicts continuous gene expression dynamics from scRNA-seq data to elucidate heterogeneity of cancer treatment responses.
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) profiles cellular heterogeneity but captures only static snapshots, limiting inference of gene expression dynamics. We developed PROFET (particle-based reconstruction of generative force-matched expression trajectories), a framework that reconstructs continuous, nonlinear single-cell trajectories from sparsely sampled scRNA-seq time series. PROFET combines a particle-based gradient-flow algorithm with simulation-free force matching to accurately infer cellular dynamics. Across mouse and human in vitro datasets and an in vivo axolotl regeneration dataset, PROFET achieved 2.6-12.5× lower prediction error than ten state-of-the-art trajectory inference methods. Applying PROFET to newly generated scRNA-seq data from a palbociclib-treated MCF7 cell line and three published breast cancer patient datasets, we reconstructed treatment-response trajectories and identified a resistant cell subpopulation exhibiting large phenotypic shifts and enrichment of the surface markers UNC5B, TLR3, PCDH19, PROCR, SLITRK6, and SEMA6B. PROFET provides a biologically grounded framework for reconstructing cell-state dynamics from static single-cell data across development, regeneration, and therapeutic response. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

bioinfo.title: Context-Aware Protein Representations Using Protein Language Models and Optimal Transport
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Proteins have different functions in different contexts. As a result, representations that take into account a protein’s biological context would allow for a more accurate assessment of its functions and properties. Protein language models (PLMs) generate amino-acid-level (residue-level) embeddings of proteins and are a powerful approach for creating universal protein representations. However, PLMs on their own do not consider context and cannot generate context-specific protein representations. We introduce COPTER, a method that uses optimal transport to pool together a protein’s PLM-generated residue-level embeddings using a separate context embedding to create context-aware protein representations. We conceptualize the residue-level embeddings as samples from a probabilistic distribution, and use sliced Wasserstein distances to map these samples against a context-specific reference set, yielding a contextualized protein-level embedding. We evaluate COPTER’s performance on three downstream prediction tasks: therapeutic drug target prediction, genetic perturbation response prediction, and TCR-epitope binding prediction. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, COPTER achieves substantially improved, near-perfect performance in predicting therapeutic targets across cell contexts. It also results in improved performance in predicting responses to genetic perturbations and binding between TCRs and epitopes. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/SahilP113/COPTER .

bioinfo.title: Optimal transport for generating transition states in chemical reactions
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Transition states (TSs) are transient structures that are key to understanding reaction mechanisms and designing catalysts but challenging to capture in experiments. Many optimization algorithms have been developed to search for TSs computationally. Yet, the cost of these algorithms driven by quantum chemistry methods (usually density functional theory) is still high, posing challenges for their applications in building large reaction networks for reaction exploration. Here we developed React-OT, an optimal transport approach for generating unique TS structures from reactants and products. React-OT generates highly accurate TS structures with a median structural root mean square deviation of 0.053 Å and median barrier height error of 1.06 kcal mol −1 requiring only 0.4 s per reaction. The root mean square deviation and barrier height error are further improved by roughly 25% through pretraining React-OT on a large reaction dataset obtained with a lower level of theory, GFN2-xTB. We envision that the remarkable accuracy and rapid inference of React-OT will be highly useful when integrated with the current high-throughput TS search workflow. This integration will facilitate the exploration of chemical reactions with unknown mechanisms.

bioinfo.title: Calibrating developmental dynamics from single-cell atlases: lineage paths outrun least-action routes
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell atlases infer developmental dynamics from destructive snapshots, yet how far realized lineage paths depart from such inferred dynamics has never been measured with controls. We introduce LADD (Least-Action Developmental Dynamics), a measurement framework that learns a stochastic developmental vector field from time-series single-cell RNA-seq and computes minimum-action and minimum-time paths, together with a three-layer calibration protocol that separates genuine path deviation from the generic cost of centroid measurement, and we compare its forecasting component with optimal-transport and flow-matching methods. In the lineage-resolved Caenorhabditis elegans atlas, the raw action ratio of observed lineage-centroid trajectories to optimal paths is 3.79, yet forward-simulated ensembles of the learned model itself score 2.07, leaving a genuine excess of about two-fold. In zebrafish ( Danio rerio ), the observed ratio sits entirely at the model’s floor. Three mechanisms that could explain the residual deviation (detours, flow-opposition, and fate-map complexity) are each excluded; what remains is speed, with lineages moving 30–43% faster along the learned flow. We report validity boundaries for temporal resolution, cross-species comparison, and energetic interpretation, delimiting where action-based trajectory comparisons are meaningful. Author Summary Embryos develop from a single cell into many specialized cell types, and modern atlases let researchers watch this process as a movie of molecular snapshots. Because each cell is measured only once, software must stitch snapshots into “trajectories”, and some studies ask whether development follows optimal routes, such as paths of least action (a principle borrowed from physics). Here we provide LADD, a method that learns the dynamics of development from such atlases and computes the optimal paths those dynamics imply, together with a calibration protocol that distinguishes genuine biological deviation from artifacts created by measuring averages of cell populations. Applying it to worm and zebrafish embryogenesis, we find that most of the apparent deviation from optimality is such a measurement artifact; what remains in the worm is a modest, genuine excess arising because lineages move faster than the optimal route, not around it. LADD offers a reusable way to test optimality claims about development against an explicit noise floor.

bioinfo.title: SPARK: Bayesian Structure Learning of Enhancer-based Gene Regulatory Networks from Single-cell Multiomics Data and Prior Knowledge
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Enhancer-based gene regulatory networks (eGRNs) linking enhancers with recruited transcription factors (TFs) and downstream target genes can help decipher complex regulatory mechanisms, such as the function of GWAS variants at enhancers. Molecular assays that profile gene expression and chromatin state jointly from the same cells (such as 10x Multiome) are a rich source of input data for eGRN reconstruction. However, these assays lack mechanistic evidence for enhancer-gene and TF-enhancer links, which can be contributed by prior knowledge from other assays and analyses. Here, we present SPARK, an eGRN reconstruction framework that formally combines single-cell multiome data with mechanistic prior knowledge. SPARK represents eGRNs as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and learns them using Bayesian inference, with a prior on the network structure constructed from heterogeneous sources of evidence. In a simulation study, we show that SPARK benefits from prior knowledge and outperforms existing DAG-based and regression-based algorithms. Finally, we use SPARK to study the regulatory circuitry of enhancers harboring immune disease GWAS variants in human primary monocytes, revealing known and novel regulatory links as candidates for experimental validation.

bioinfo.title: Abstract B010: Evolutionary reconstruction of CRISPR-programmable regulatory circuits reveals gene therapy vulnerabilities in recurrent glioblastoma
bioinfo.abstract: GBM) is driven by dynamic rewiring of gene regulatory networks that promote mesenchymal evolution and treatment escape. However, most computational approaches reconstruct static regulatory architectures and fail to identify temporal intervention points suitable for programmable gene therapy. We developed a computational framework that integrates single-cell transcriptomics, gene regulatory network inference, evolutionary trajectory reconstruction, and CRISPR perturbation modeling to identify regulatory vulnerabilities that emerge during recurrent GBM progression. Single-cell RNA sequencing datasets comprising approximately 8,000 cells per tumor were integrated with publicly available recurrent GBM cohorts to reconstruct lineage-specific transcriptional trajectories. Regulatory interactions were inferred across approximately 20,000 genes, generating a network of over 120,000 predicted transcription factor-enhancer interactions. Evolutionary trajectory analysis identified progressive regulatory rewiring associated with transition from proneural to mesenchymal cell states. Network centrality analysis and simulated CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) perturbations were used to prioritize combinations of transcription factors and enhancer elements predicted to destabilize resistance-associated regulatory programs. The computational framework identified 19 regulatory hubs demonstrating progressive activation during recurrent disease and 31 enhancer elements selectively associated with mesenchymal transition. Simulated combinatorial CRISPR perturbation prioritized 14 transcription factor-enhancer pairs predicted to produce substantially greater disruption of mesenchymal regulatory signaling than single-target interventions. Network simulations predicted a 42% reduction in regulatory connectivity within resistance-associated modules following combinatorial perturbation, with the highest-ranked targets converging on established GBM regulators including STAT3, CEBPB, FOSL2, and RUNX1. Independent validation across external recurrent GBM datasets demonstrated reproducible prioritization of key regulatory circuits despite interpatient heterogeneity. These findings suggest that recurrent GBM evolution is sustained by temporally acquired regulatory dependencies that can be computationally identified before experimental perturbation. By integrating evolutionary trajectory reconstruction with programmable CRISPR regulatory modeling, this framework identifies candidate gene therapy strategies designed to collapse mesenchymal evolution rather than target individual downstream genes. The approach provides a scalable computational platform for prioritizing combinatorial regulatory interventions in recurrent glioblastoma and may be broadly applicable to other cancers characterized by dynamic transcriptional plasticity and therapeutic resistance. bulk2scDiff: A Pseudobulk-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Bulk-to-Single-Cell RNA-Seq Generation
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Bulk RNA sequencing remains the predominant profiling strategy for large clinical cohorts, but it aggregates transcriptional signals across cell populations, thereby masking the underlying cellular heterogeneity. Inferring this heterogeneity from existing bulk transcriptomic data could extend large cohort-based studies that have already been profiled, but constitutes an underdetermined inverse problem, as one bulk profile can be compatible with multiple underlying cellular populations. Existing computational deconvolution methods address this problem primarily by estimating cell-type proportions or cell-type-averaged expression profiles rather than resolving expression at the level of individual cells. Here, we present bulk2scDiff, a proof-of-concept conditional diffusion framework that reformulates bulk-to-single-cell inference as conditional generation of single-cell expression profiles from pseudobulk transcriptomic input. We evaluated bulk2scDiff on two cancer single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, breast cancer and acute myeloid leukemia, where pseudobulk profiles were derived from the single-cell data and used as conditioning inputs, with the matched single-cell populations providing ground truth for controlled evaluation. Across both cases, bulk2scDiff closely reconstructed populations from training samples and generated biologically coherent single-cell populations for held-out samples, generalizing most consistently to recurrent immune features. A pseudobulk-swap control further confirmed sample-specific conditioning, with each sample’s corresponding pseudobulk yielding the closest agreement with its observed population in nearly all cases. Overall, our work establishes the feasibility of conditional diffusion for generating single-cell populations from pseudobulk transcriptomic profiles, providing a foundation for future evaluation with clinical bulk RNA sequencing data.

bioinfo.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS.
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

bioinfo.title: S100A11 sustains STRAP stability to drive PI3K/AKT/NF-κB feedforward signalling circuit activation in colorectal cancer progression.
bioinfo.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide, with persistently low rates of early-stage diagnosis, poor overall prognosis, and a propensity for therapeutic resistance-challenges that underscore the urgent need for deeper mechanistic insight. By integrating single-cell transcriptomic data (GSE161277) with multi-omics datasets from TCGA and GEO repositories, alongside an independent clinical cohort, we identified S100A11 as a consistently overexpressed gene in CRC that correlates significantly with adverse patient outcomes. Functional studies established that S100A11 drives tumour progression by promoting cell proliferation, suppressing apoptosis, and inducing epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Mechanistically, S100A11 engages the WD6-7 domain (residues 221-302) of STRAP through direct physical interaction, thereby recruiting the deubiquitylase OTUB1 to shield lysine K246 of STRAP from K63-linked polyubiquitination. This protection stabilises STRAP and facilitates its association with PI3K, culminating in activation of the PI3K/AKT/NF-κB cascade and nuclear translocation of p65. We further demonstrate that p65 binds directly to the promoter regions of both S100A11 and STRAP, transcriptionally upregulating their expression and establishing a self-reinforcing feedforward loop that sustains pathway activation. Collectively, these findings delineate a hierarchical regulatory network centred on the S100A11/STRAP/NF-κB axis and offer a mechanistic framework with potential implications for CRC diagnosis and targeted intervention.

bioinfo.title: VCBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Single-Cell Foundation Models
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell foundation models are increasingly positioned as virtual cells, yet their capabilities are assessed by fragmented, largely single-task benchmarks that obscure where these models improve on simple baselines. VCBench addresses this by synthesizing four independent virtual-cell frameworks into seven capability dimensions: perturbation response prediction, cross-species universality, gene regulatory network (GRN) inference, modality integration, temporal dynamics, multi-scale integration, and in silico experimentation. Each dimension is assessed for operational testability under current architectures and datasets: five admit direct or proxy evaluation, while multi-scale integration and in silico experimentation are structurally untestable as end-to-end tasks. We evaluate five foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT, UCE, TranscriptFormer, Arc State) against pre-registered linear and nearest-neighbor baselines across the five testable dimensions, and report three findings. First, the baselines match or exceed every foundation model on four of the five scored dimensions, replicating the reported competitiveness of linear baselines on perturbation prediction and extending it to cross-species transfer, GRN inference, and temporal ordering. Second, TranscriptFormer alone exceeds the strongest baseline on cross-modal RNA-to-protein prediction (53% Pearson improvement, with a documented contamination caveat) and is the only model to reach Level 2 in the pre-registered Virtual Cell (VC) Level rubric; the architectural choice behind this advantage simultaneously causes a spectral collapse that destroys its temporal-ordering performance, a tradeoff invisible to single-task benchmarks. Third, no foundation model publishes a complete cell-level training manifest, leaving data contamination undetectable to users. Alongside the benchmark, VCBench releases a Contamination Reporting Schema and contributes two further methodological tools: a common-label-set protocol that controls for class-count confounds in cross-species transfer, and a spread-error correlation probe for epistemic calibration.

bioinfo.title: SPECHTacle: An Efficient Detection and Visualization of Cell Specific Regulation in Single Cell-Based Experiments Using a Novel Combinatorial Computational Tool
bioinfo.abstract: ABSTRACT Herein, we describe SPECHTacle, a novel computational tool affording the ability to efficiently visualize and delineate the specific cellular population(s) impacted by an experimental paradigm utilizing heterogeneous cell-based samples. SPECHTacle can be employed to efficiently determine, in a cell specific manner, the populations preferentially impacted by treatments, drugs, injuries, disease states, and/or development within datasets continuously being generated across nearly countless subfields in molecular biology. SPECHTacle accomplishes this task by harnessing the power of Waddington optimal transport analysis and Shannon entropy in a combinatorial fashion to distinguish cell populations preferentially altered due to nearly any experimental paradigm and generates a visual representation of cellular entropy (i.e. change) across entire datasets. Ultimately, this allows for efficient determination of specific populations preferentially impacted by an experimental paradigm and identifies populations to target for downstream analyses employing quantitative measurements. We propose that SPECHTacle represents an immediately useful computational tool with the potential to be integrated into single cell-based workflows and greatly enhance the efficiency of both manual and machine-based learning workflows.

bioinfo.title: scTransMIL bridges patient-level disease states and single-cell transcriptomics for cancer screening and heterogeneity inference.
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell sequencing offers profound insights into tumor complexity. However, reliably linking individual cellular profiles to overall sample-level phenotypes remains computationally challenging, particularly when cell-specific annotations are absent. This disconnect limits the technology's utility in studying underlying tumor mechanisms. Here we show how scTransMIL, an artificial intelligence framework, bridges this gap. By conceptualizing a biological sample as a collection of individual cells, scTransMIL employs a transformer-based multi-instance learning approach to directly connect single-cell transcriptomic profiles with overarching sample-level labels. We demonstrate that scTransMIL accurately predicts sample-level cancer phenotypes, including the tissue-of-origin for metastatic tumors. At cellular resolution, it robustly identifies tumor-associated cell populations and maps biological progression trajectories using only minimal sample-level annotations. Furthermore, the model's attention mechanisms facilitate full-transcriptome biomarker discovery. By systematically integrating molecular and cellular scales with broader phenotypic states, our approach provides a computational tool to dissect tumor heterogeneity and advance fundamental cancer biology.
